results.reader_title: A proposed German fibre backbone for sharing quantum and precision-timing signals nationwide
results.reader_what: Researchers propose a ten-year, four-phase national dark-fibre backbone distributing quantum and precise time signals.
results.reader_why: Such capability currently reaches only a few institutions, limiting European research access and industrial deployment.
results.reader_more: This is a white paper setting out a design, not a funded or built system. The authors, from German metrology and research-networking institutions, propose dedicated unlit optical fibre carrying quantum signals and reference time and frequency signals between laboratories and companies. They argue the underlying links are already demonstrated at high technical maturity, citing existing German connections, the REFIMEVE network in France and Italy's LIFT network. The rollout is planned in four phases over ten years to widen access beyond today's isolated testbeds. Whether it is built depends on national funding decisions the paper itself cannot settle.

deep_analysis.research_question: How could Germany move quantum and time-and-frequency signal distribution beyond isolated testbeds into shared national infrastructure?
deep_analysis.main_finding: The authors propose a dedicated national dark-fibre backbone, deployed in four phases over ten years, arguing the component links are already proven at high technology readiness elsewhere in Europe.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Design proposal by a multi-institution author group, building on demonstrated fibre links (PTB-MPQ, REFIMEVE, LIFT); publisher open-access full text supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: A proposal only: no deployment, funding commitment or independent evaluation is reported, and the ten-year phasing is intended rather than agreed.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Concerns European research infrastructure for quantum technology and for resilient timing, including reducing dependence on satellite navigation signals.

results.reader_title: EU agrees a €115 million programme to speed disruptive defence technology to the field
results.reader_what: Parliament and Council reached political agreement on AGILE, aimed at smaller firms and operational from January 2027.
results.reader_why: Delivers disruptive defence products to member states and associated countries, including Ukraine.
results.reader_more: This is a political agreement between the European Parliament and the Council, reached on 15 July 2026, and not yet final adopted legislation. The Commission proposed AGILE in March 2026 with a budget of €115 million, directed at small and medium-sized enterprises, start-ups and scale-ups rather than established defence primes. Work is to be organised around mission-driven challenges defined with member states, with the stated ambition of developing, testing and deploying products in weeks or months instead of years. The instrument is expected to be operational from 1 January 2027, with continuity intended through the proposed European Competitiveness Fund. The delivery timescales described are programme objectives, not demonstrated performance.

deep_analysis.main_finding: The European Parliament and Council reached political agreement on 15 July 2026 on AGILE, a €115 million programme to accelerate development, testing and uptake of disruptive defence technologies from smaller and newer suppliers, enabling launch in early 2027.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Primary source: European Commission Directorate-General for Defence Industry and Space announcement; page text supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: Political agreement stage rather than adopted law; budget, start date and the weeks-to-months delivery ambition are commitments and objectives, not observed results.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: A new EU instrument channelling defence innovation funding to SMEs and start-ups, linked to European Defence Readiness 2030 and technological sovereignty aims.

results.reader_title: Does the EU's digital sovereignty agenda widen divides between its core and periphery?
results.reader_what: Article argues initiatives meant to secure Europe externally may deepen digital divides inside the Union.
results.reader_why: Identifies a paradox internal to the EU's own digital sovereignty agenda.
results.reader_more: The author examines how the EU's pursuit of digital sovereignty interacts with inequalities that already exist between member states. The central claim is a paradox: measures designed to make Europe more sovereign, secure and competitive against outside powers may work against cohesion within the Union and contribute to widening digital divides between core and peripheral member states. The author is explicit that results are not uniform across the cases considered. This interpretation rests on the published abstract alone, since the publisher page was blocked to the scanner and online recovery did not reach the full text. The study's methods, case selection and evidence base therefore could not be verified.

deep_analysis.research_question: How does the EU's pursuit of digital sovereignty relate to existing intra-European inequalities between core and periphery?
deep_analysis.main_finding: The agenda contains an inherent paradox: initiatives intended to make Europe sovereign, secure and competitive against external powers may produce opposite effects internally, contributing to growing digital divides, though the author notes results are not uniform.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Abstract only. Package source retrieval failed with a 403 from the publisher, and targeted online searching located the article record but not an accessible abstract page or repository copy.
deep_analysis.qualification: Method, cases and evidence base could not be established; the finding above is the abstract's own summary statement, and the author explicitly qualifies that results vary.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Concerns whether EU digital sovereignty policy reinforces or reduces inequality between member states, a cohesion question inside a flagship agenda.

results.reader_title: How a middle power balances AI innovation against regulatory control: the case of Türkiye
results.reader_what: A legal case study argues AI sovereignty spans technical capacity, regulation and strategic positioning together.
results.reader_why: Treats the EU AI Act as the benchmark against which Türkiye's regulatory choices are assessed.
results.reader_more: The authors use Türkiye as a case for how states outside the large AI powers try to keep meaningful control over infrastructure, data, rules and technical capability at once. They set the country's approach against a comparison of global regulatory models, taking the EU AI Act as the first comprehensive benchmark and contrasting precautionary and self-regulatory styles. Their argument is that sovereignty in this field cannot be reduced to one dimension, so governance has to stay adaptable. This is legal and policy analysis rather than measurement: it offers an interpretation of strategy documents and regulation, not evidence about outcomes.

deep_analysis.research_question: How does a middle power such as Türkiye reconcile AI innovation with regulatory control while maintaining strategic autonomy?
deep_analysis.main_finding: AI sovereignty is multi-dimensional, covering technical capability, regulatory frameworks and strategic positioning, and therefore requires adaptable rather than single-track governance approaches.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Single-country case study with comparative review of global AI regulatory frameworks; publisher abstract and full text supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: Interpretive analysis of strategy and regulation; no empirical measurement of effects, and conclusions are specific to one country's position.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Shows how Europe's AI rulebook functions as an external benchmark for neighbouring states positioning between European and other regulatory models.

results.reader_title: UKRI's five-year strategy: discovery research, government priorities and helping companies scale
results.reader_what: Strategy organises over £9 billion of annual investment around five priorities, including keeping scaling companies in Britain.
results.reader_why: UKRI describes itself as the largest national research and innovation investor in Europe.
results.reader_more: This is a strategy document, so it states intentions rather than results. Its five parts cover support for discovery and curiosity-driven research, addressing strategic government and societal priorities, helping companies start, scale and stay in the UK, strengthening the foundations of the research system, and reforming UKRI itself. The framing throughout is that curiosity-driven research and commercial application reinforce one another rather than compete for the same money. The organisation reports being entrusted with more than £9 billion of public funding each year, spanning arts, humanities and social sciences through to physics and engineering. Whether the commitments are met depends on future funding settlements and delivery, neither of which a strategy can settle.

deep_analysis.main_finding: UKRI sets out a 2026-2031 strategy structured around five objectives: supporting discovery research, addressing strategic government and societal priorities, helping companies start, scale and stay in the UK, strengthening research system foundations, and reforming its own organisation.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Primary source: the published UKRI strategy document; PDF text supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: A statement of intent for 2026-2031 rather than evidence of performance; no outcomes are reported and delivery depends on future funding settlements.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Sets the five-year direction of what the document describes as Europe's largest national research and innovation investor.

results.reader_title: Why AI rules written for tools miss AI's role as shared infrastructure
results.reader_what: Reviewing six governance instruments, the paper argues they regulate what AI does, not what it makes thinkable.
results.reader_why: The EU AI Act is among the six instruments said to leave this gap unaddressed.
results.reader_more: This is a conceptual argument rather than an empirical study. The author separates the properties of a tool, which is visible, optional and bounded to a task, from those of infrastructure, which is invisible, effectively unavoidable and shapes what can be thought at all. Six frameworks from North America, Europe and Asia are assessed against that distinction, including the EU AI Act, the United States NIST risk management framework and China's rules for generative services. The claimed gap is that each addresses identifiable harms, transparency and oversight, but none addresses how these systems shape the information people reason with. The proposed remedies are sketched in principle and have not been tested or adopted.

deep_analysis.research_question: Do AI governance frameworks built on a tool model remain adequate once AI systems function as infrastructure?
deep_analysis.main_finding: A systematic regulatory gap is identified: the six instruments examined address AI system behaviour and harms but not AI's role in shaping the conditions of thought, which the author terms epistemic infrastructure.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Conceptual framework distinguishing tool from infrastructure properties, applied as a structured comparison of six governance instruments; publisher open-access full text supplied.
deep_analysis.qualification: The gap is argued conceptually rather than demonstrated empirically, and the proposed governance mechanisms are untested.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Directly evaluates the EU AI Act alongside other major regimes and proposes a different regulatory logic for foundational AI systems.

results.reader_title: Moving EU tokenised securities trading from a temporary sandbox to a permanent regime
results.reader_what: The article argues the DLT pilot regime's low size caps and missing cash settlement limited its uptake.
results.reader_why: Authors tie the successor framework's success to European technological sovereignty and national-level supervision.
results.reader_more: Distributed ledger technology here means shared digital record-keeping that allows securities to be settled and split into smaller units. The authors trace the EU's 2022 pilot regime, a temporary sandbox for trading and settling tokenised instruments, and argue that restrictive capitalisation thresholds and the absence of an integrated cash leg held adoption down. They then assess the Commission's Market Integration and Supervision Package, which would make the arrangement permanent, unbundle central securities depository services into new notary and account-keeping roles, and raise aggregate thresholds to one hundred billion euros. The package is a legislative proposal under negotiation, so its effects are anticipated rather than observed.

deep_analysis.research_question: Why did the EU's DLT Pilot Regime see limited uptake, and does the proposed successor framework fix the causes?
deep_analysis.main_finding: The pilot regime carried a built-in ceiling on success through restrictive capitalisation thresholds and lack of native cash settlement; the proposed Market Integration and Supervision Package addresses these through unbundled depository roles and far higher thresholds.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Doctrinal analysis of Regulation (EU) 2022/858, ESMA's 2025 recommendations and the Commission proposal, with contrasting project cases; publisher full text supplied.
deep_analysis.qualification: The successor package is a proposal still in the legislative process, so claimed benefits are projected, and the sovereignty and supervision conclusions are the authors' argument rather than findings.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Concerns whether Europe's financial market infrastructure is built and supervised in Europe, which the authors frame as a technological sovereignty question.

results.reader_title: Europe leads the science of biomanufacturing but risks losing the industry to China
results.reader_what: Report argues Europe leads biomanufacturing patents and research but lacks scale-up infrastructure and faces regulatory delay.
results.reader_why: Repeats the solar, battery and electric vehicle pattern: Europe invents, others capture the manufacturing.
results.reader_more: Biomanufacturing here means using engineered microbes to make fuels, chemicals, materials and food that currently come from fossil resources. The report's case is that cheap renewable electricity and AI-guided biology are turning this from a niche climate option into a general production method. It cites China holding more than seventy per cent of global basic fermentation capacity, spending an estimated two to three billion euros a year on biotechnology research, and targeting global bioeconomy leadership by 2035. Europe is credited with leading patents, specialised clusters and competitive firms, but faulted for thin scale-up capacity and slow regulatory decisions. This is advocacy from a foreign policy think tank rather than peer-reviewed analysis, and the figures are its own compilation.

deep_analysis.research_question: Can Europe convert its lead in biomanufacturing science into industrial and geopolitical advantage before China consolidates the sector?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Europe leads in patents and core technologies but is constrained by limited scale-up infrastructure, regulatory delay and growing dependence on Chinese manufacturing capacity, while China treats biomanufacturing as a state strategic priority alongside AI.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Policy analysis drawing on Chinese planning documents, public investment estimates and industrial capacity figures; publisher web text supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: Advocacy-oriented and not peer-reviewed; investment figures are estimates and the competitive outcome is a projection rather than an observed result.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Frames biomanufacturing as the next industrial and strategic autonomy race and names specific European weaknesses in scale-up and regulation.

results.reader_title: How EU de-risking is turning research cooperation with China into a security question
results.reader_what: Cooperation structures largely persist but are increasingly overlaid with eligibility rules, risk screening and interference guidance.
results.reader_why: Directly concerns Horizon Europe participation rules and the 2024 Council recommendation on research security.
results.reader_more: The authors read EU policy documents from 2021 to 2025, including the Horizon Europe participation rules, the European Economic Security Strategy and the 2024 Council recommendation on research security, alongside Chinese ministry readouts and state media commentary. They describe a dual trajectory in which formal cooperation architectures and dialogues survive, but are progressively layered with security conditions that narrow who may take part and on what terms. They also track Chinese counter-narratives of openness and reciprocity that contest the legitimacy of these moves. Because this is a qualitative reading of public documents, it establishes how the framing and the policy toolkit developed, not what effect either has had on actual collaboration volumes or research output.

deep_analysis.research_question: How is the EU's de-risking agenda reconfiguring the governance of research cooperation with China between 2021 and 2025?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Research security has been constructed as a governance category and translated into concrete eligibility rules, screening and safeguarding guidance layered on top of cooperation structures that themselves remain in place, while Chinese actors mount counter-narratives contesting that framing.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Securitisation theory applied through qualitative analysis of EU policy documents and Chinese official and state-media material; publisher open-access full text supplied.
deep_analysis.qualification: Document-based interpretation covering discourse and instruments; it does not measure effects on collaboration volumes, funding flows or research output.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Traces how research security conditions entered Horizon Europe participation rules and EU research governance more broadly.

results.reader_title: Do US, EU and UN artificial intelligence rules answer the concerns experts raised?
results.reader_what: Content analysis finds EU, Biden-era and UN frameworks reflect expert concerns; corporate power concentration is largely sidelined.
results.reader_why: The EU AI Act is one of four frameworks assessed and shares the corporate-power blind spot.
results.reader_more: The benchmark is the open letter calling for a pause on giant AI experiments, treated as a summary of expert concern. Four documents are compared against it: two United States executive orders from the Trump and Biden administrations, the EU AI Act, and the United Nations report Governing AI for Humanity. The authors judge the market-oriented Trump order to deflect most of those concerns, while the Biden order, the EU Act and the UN report engage strongly with human rights, safety and accountability. The gap they highlight is concentration of corporate power, which they find addressed more fully by the UN than by Western regulation. This is qualitative document analysis, so the judgements are interpretive rather than measured.

deep_analysis.research_question: How far do major AI governance frameworks reflect the ethical concerns articulated by the AI expert community?
deep_analysis.main_finding: The Biden executive order, the EU AI Act and the UN report reflect expert concerns about rights, safety and accountability, whereas the earlier market-oriented US order refracts them; concentration of corporate power is a shared gap in Western frameworks and better covered by the UN.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Qualitative content analysis comparing four governance documents against concerns stated in the Pause Giant AI Experiments open letter; publisher full text supplied.
deep_analysis.qualification: The expert baseline is a single open letter, and reflect-versus-refract judgements are the authors' interpretation rather than a validated measure.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Assesses the EU AI Act comparatively and identifies a specific area, corporate concentration, that European rules are said to underweight.

results.reader_title: Fifty-five semiconductor insiders rate the geopolitical risks facing Europe's chip supply to 2031
results.reader_what: Respondents rank export controls on key manufacturing inputs and military conflict over Taiwan as the severest threats.
results.reader_why: Without chip access Europe cannot sustain its medical, defence and other critical industries.
results.reader_more: Fifty-five respondents, predominantly from the semiconductor industry and research and technology organisations, anonymously scored twenty threats on two separate zero-to-ten scales, one for security of supply and one for European competitiveness. The overall picture they give for the period to late 2031 is pessimistic. Alongside export controls and Taiwan, the paper points to unfair competition and high European energy prices. Its recommendations are procedural rather than industrial: monthly risk monitoring, medium-term risk projections, and war-gaming exercises that break down silos between industry and policymakers. This is elicited expert perception rather than measured risk, and it is a first iteration with no earlier round to compare against.

deep_analysis.research_question: Which geopolitical risks to semiconductor supply and European competitiveness do ecosystem experts judge most severe through 2031?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Curtailment of key manufacturing inputs through export controls and a military conflict over Taiwan emerge as the highest-scored threats, within a generally bleak outlook for European semiconductor supply and competitiveness.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Anonymous survey of 55 industry, policy and think tank respondents scoring 20 threats on two 0-to-10 scales; PDF excerpt supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: Subjective expert perception from a predominantly industry sample, not measured probability; first iteration with no baseline, and only an excerpt of the report was available here.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Provides a structured expert risk picture for a technology the EU treats as foundational to industrial and defence capability.

results.reader_title: What applied AI startups actually need from Europe's publicly funded computing capacity
results.reader_what: Interviews in Poland find real but sector-specific demand; startups want unbureaucratic access, data protection and easy portability.
results.reader_why: Argues public AI compute should be designed for applied startups, not only frontier model training.
results.reader_more: The evidence is ten semi-structured interviews in Poland, the fourth-largest national recipient of EU AI factory funding: one AI factory host, four industry and research intermediaries, and five startups in regulated or strategic sectors such as health, life sciences, space and defence. The authors reframe the usual argument about whether public compute is justified, asking instead for whom and on what terms it works. Free access to high-performance computing is welcomed provided it is quick to obtain, protects data and intellectual property, comes with local human support, and allows switching between public facilities and commercial cloud. Gigafactories are seen as extra capacity rather than a different offer. Ten interviews in one country is a narrow base, so these are indicative requirements.

deep_analysis.work_kind: policy brief based on qualitative interviews
deep_analysis.research_question: For whom, in what form and under what conditions can publicly funded AI compute support European AI development?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Demand from applied AI startups in regulated and strategic sectors is genuine but sector-specific, and public compute converts into value mainly when access is fast and unbureaucratic, protects data and intellectual property, provides local support and data, and permits movement between public and commercial providers.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Ten semi-structured interviews with an AI factory host, four ecosystem intermediaries and five startups in Poland's AI factory ecosystem; report PDF supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: Small single-country interview sample capturing stated requirements, not measured demand or realised outcomes; remaining obstacles such as national co-funding and sovereignty guarantees are unresolved.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Speaks directly to the design of EU AI factory and gigafactory investment and to the technology sovereignty case made for public compute.

results.reader_title: A new measure of how steadily countries turn research spending into innovation output
results.reader_what: Across thirty countries, measured innovation efficiency stays below 0.25, with East Asia ahead of Europe.
results.reader_why: Places Europe behind East Asia and the Pacific at converting research inputs into innovation outputs.
results.reader_more: Efficiency here is a ratio rather than a level: it asks how much innovation a country gets from the inputs it puts in, so a small system can score well while producing little in absolute terms. The authors add a second measure, sustainable innovation efficiency, meant to capture whether output holds steady when inputs fluctuate. Using data envelopment analysis on thirty countries from 2009 to 2018, they find high-income countries do better on the stability measure while lower-middle-income countries score highest on plain efficiency. The regional comparison puts East Asia and the Pacific ahead of Europe and Central Asia. Results of this method depend heavily on which inputs and outputs are chosen, and the data window closes in 2018.

deep_analysis.research_question: How efficiently do countries convert R&D inputs into innovation outputs, and how stable is that conversion when inputs are volatile?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Overall innovation efficiency is low across the sample, consistently below 0.25; high-income countries lead on the new sustainable-efficiency measure while lower-middle-income countries lead on conventional efficiency, and East Asia and the Pacific outperform Europe and Central Asia on the latter.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Data envelopment analysis of 30 countries, 2009-2018, introducing a sustainable innovation efficiency measure alongside conventional innovation efficiency; publisher open-access full text supplied.
deep_analysis.qualification: Efficiency is relative to the chosen input and output variables and says nothing about absolute innovation capacity; the sample ends in 2018 and covers 30 countries only.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Offers a comparative benchmark placing European performance against East Asia in converting research investment into output.

results.reader_title: Why concentrated AI investment leaves the EU dependent on technology developed elsewhere
results.reader_what: Article argues United States private AI investment dwarfs the EU's while transfer channels deepen European technological dependence.
results.reader_why: Frames a strategic choice for the EU between remaining a technology consumer or becoming a producer.
results.reader_more: The article reports that in 2024 private AI investment in the United States exceeded the EU's by roughly fifteen to twenty times, with Europe's share of global AI investment still falling. It maps the channels through which American multinationals transfer AI technology into Europe and argues these bring real benefits while entrenching reliance on outside solutions. European regulation is described as cutting both ways, protecting markets and consumers but adding compliance costs that weigh more heavily on startups than on large firms. The priorities it recommends are domestic AI infrastructure, support for innovative enterprises, retaining skilled people and clearer investment transparency. This is an analytical review built on published figures rather than new estimation, and the headline investment ratio is given as an approximate range.

deep_analysis.research_question: How does asymmetric international investment in AI, and the technology transfer channels that accompany it, shape EU technological dependence?
deep_analysis.main_finding: AI investment is concentrated in a few global hubs; transfer channels from United States multinationals deliver benefits to European economies while reinforcing dependence on externally developed technology, leaving the EU facing a choice between consuming and producing AI technology.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Conceptual and descriptive analysis of published investment statistics and technology transfer channels; publisher abstract and article text supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: Secondary statistics and reasoned argument rather than tested estimation; the dependence mechanism is argued, not measured, and the investment gap is cited as a broad range.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Concerns the investment basis of European AI capability and the strategic autonomy consequences of relying on foreign technology suppliers.

results.reader_title: What the European Research Council's Proof of Concept grants have produced since 2014
results.reader_what: Report finds Proof of Concept grantees at least five times likelier to file patents than main-grant-only holders.
results.reader_why: Grantees secured over €200 million in follow-on EIC Transition funding, nearly half of successful applicants.
results.reader_more: Proof of Concept grants are small follow-on awards, open only to existing ERC grant holders, supporting prototyping, market validation, patenting and stakeholder engagement. Between 2014 and 2023 the scheme funded 1,731 projects across 30 EU and associated countries, an investment of €259 million. Health biotechnology and medical technology account for 43 per cent of the portfolio, followed by advanced materials at 17 per cent, artificial intelligence and information technology at 13 per cent and quantum technologies at 12 per cent. The report is produced by the ERC's own executive agency and reviewed by its innovation working group, so it is self-assessment rather than independent evaluation. The patenting comparison does not adjust for the fact that grantees apply and are selected competitively.

deep_analysis.research_question: What innovation activity and follow-on investment has the ERC Proof of Concept scheme generated from frontier research?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Across 1,731 projects and €259 million between 2014 and 2023, the portfolio is concentrated in health and medical technology, with grantees at least five times more likely to file patents than ERC main-grant-only holders and accounting for nearly half of successful EIC Transition applicants, drawing over €200 million in follow-on funding.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Descriptive portfolio analysis of ERC Proof of Concept projects prepared by the ERC Executive Agency and reviewed by the ERC Working Group on Innovation; report PDF supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: Self-assessment by the funding body; the patenting and follow-on funding comparisons are descriptive and do not account for self-selection and competitive selection into the scheme, so they are not causal effects.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Provides portfolio evidence on how EU frontier research funding translates into patents, companies and follow-on investment, central to the competitiveness debate.

results.reader_title: How EU research funding supports work on democracy, governance and disinformation
results.reader_what: Commission page reports about 30% of Cluster 2's budget of over €2 billion supports democracy research.
results.reader_why: Links Horizon Europe funding to the European Democracy Shield adopted in November 2025.
results.reader_more: This is an institutional information page rather than a study, so its function is to describe the funding landscape. It places the work alongside the European Democracy Shield, the Commission communication adopted in November 2025 covering freedom of expression, institutions, elections, free media, citizen engagement and foreign information manipulation and interference. The dedicated intervention area on democracy and governance sits within Cluster 2 of Horizon Europe, and the page notes that the predecessor programme Horizon 2020 invested over €600 million across almost 200 projects in this field. Attitudinal figures cited on the page come from Eurobarometer surveys. The page sets out allocations and intentions and does not evaluate what the funded research achieved.

deep_analysis.main_finding: Horizon Europe maintains a dedicated democracy and governance intervention area within Cluster 2, with around 30% of that cluster's budget of more than €2 billion directed at strengthening democratic governance, building on over €600 million and nearly 200 projects under Horizon 2020.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Primary institutional source: European Commission Research and Innovation web page describing funding lines, strategic plans and Eurobarometer evidence; page text supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: Descriptive programme information, not an evaluation; budget shares are as stated by the Commission and no outcomes or impacts of the funded research are assessed.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Documents the scale and policy anchoring of EU research funding on democratic resilience, including its link to the European Democracy Shield.

results.reader_title: Council sets its partial negotiating position on the EU's next research framework programme
results.reader_what: Position gives member states a stronger priority-setting role and strengthens research security and dual-use provisions.
results.reader_why: Sets the Council's mandate for negotiations with Parliament on the 2028-2034 framework programme.
results.reader_more: The position is explicitly partial: financial and broader horizontal questions remain tied to the wider 2028-2034 budget negotiation, and elements concerning the European Institute of Innovation and Technology are excluded pending separate proposals. It covers the regulation establishing the programme together with its participation and dissemination rules, and the Council decision on the specific programme that implements it. Substantively the Council proposes a four-pillar structure, closer links to the proposed European Competitiveness Fund, stronger provisions on European Partnerships, research security and dual-use or limited defence-related applications, simpler cost and reporting arrangements, and continued support for widening participation. None of this is settled, since the text now serves as a mandate for talks with the European Parliament.

deep_analysis.main_finding: The Council agreed a partial negotiating position on the next framework programme, giving member states a greater role in strategic priority-setting, reorganising the programme into four pillars, tightening research security provisions and opening space for dual-use and limited defence-related applications.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Institutional news summary by the ERA Portal Austria of the Council's partial general approach; page text supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: A negotiating mandate rather than a final decision: budget and horizontal issues remain open, EIT elements are excluded, and this is a secondary summary rather than the Council text itself.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Concerns the design, governance and security rules of the EU's next research and innovation framework programme for 2028-2034.

results.reader_title: Four scenarios for Europe's growth model in an age of strategic capitalism
results.reader_what: Paper argues the EU's growth model relies on externally sourced inputs and technologies, leaving it structurally fragile.
results.reader_why: Only one of four scenarios, Strategic Europe, aligns competitiveness, control and innovation direction.
results.reader_more: Strategic capitalism here describes an environment in which industrial policy, investment screening and export controls have become ordinary instruments of statecraft. The authors argue that Europe's current model, built on externally sourced inputs, technologies and infrastructures, is fragile under those conditions, and that its innovation future depends on aligning competitiveness with control over critical economic flows and a clear direction for innovation. They set out four trajectories: Dependent Europe, innovation without control or direction; Fortress Europe, control without dynamism; Fragmented Europe, ambition without alignment; and Strategic Europe, which aligns all three and is the only one they see leading to sustained technological leadership. The scenarios are analytical constructions used to structure the argument rather than predictions.

deep_analysis.research_question: What growth model does the EU need for innovation-led competitiveness under conditions of strategic capitalism?
deep_analysis.main_finding: The EU's reliance on externally sourced inputs, technologies and infrastructures makes its growth model structurally fragile; of four constructed trajectories only Strategic Europe aligns competitiveness, control over critical flows and innovation direction, which the authors argue requires stronger national and EU policy alignment.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Conceptual and scenario-based policy analysis situated in geoeconomics literature; report PDF supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: Scenario-based argument rather than empirical modelling, so the trajectories illustrate possibilities and are not forecasts. Note that the package's scanner metadata names a different author; the paper itself is by Mikael Wigell and Sinikukka Saari.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Directly addresses EU innovation policy, strategic autonomy and competitiveness, offering a scenario frame for European growth-model choices.

results.reader_title: Mapping where AI is invented, encountered and actually used across European regions
results.reader_what: Exposure and worker use are widespread, while invention and firm adoption stay concentrated in wealthy, high-skill hubs.
results.reader_why: Authors call for place-sensitive policy: support leading regions while building capability in lagging ones.
results.reader_more: The study uses six indicators across EU NUTS-2 regions, the statistical unit roughly equivalent to a province or large region, to separate three distinct things: where AI is invented, where workers and industries are exposed to it, and where it is actually used. The pattern the authors call a spatial paradox is that exposure and individual use spread fairly broadly while invention and firm-level adoption cluster in regions with high income and highly educated workforces. They describe a persistent implementation gap between structural exposure and productive use, attributed to institutional, organisational and capability frictions. Income and human capital track AI activity closely, while trade openness runs the other way. These are associations across regions, not causal estimates.

deep_analysis.research_question: How are AI innovation, exposure and use distributed across European regions, and what regional characteristics are associated with each?
deep_analysis.main_finding: A spatial paradox: AI exposure and worker-level use are relatively widespread across EU regions while innovation and firm-level adoption remain concentrated in high-GDP, human-capital-intensive hubs, leaving a persistent implementation gap between exposure and productive use driven by institutional, organisational and capability frictions.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Six complementary indicators of AI innovation, exposure and use mapped and correlated across EU NUTS-2 regions. Package contained no source text (publisher returned 403), so the abstract was recovered online from the publisher record and the JRC repository entry.
deep_analysis.qualification: Descriptive and correlational rather than causal; indicators are drawn from different reference years, and the authors state the views are their own and not an official European Commission position. Interpretation here rests on the abstract, not the full text.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Provides regional-level evidence on European AI capability and adoption gaps, directly relevant to place-based innovation and cohesion policy.

results.reader_title: Mapping what European university alliances have contributed to the European Research Area
results.reader_what: Study codes 301 outputs from 32 funded alliances by activity, audience and European Research Area action.
results.reader_why: Addresses a gap: evidence on alliances' contribution to the European Research Area remains limited.
results.reader_more: The European Universities Initiative groups universities across borders into transnational alliances. This paper takes 301 outputs from 32 alliances funded under the Science with and for Society strand of Horizon 2020 and codes each by transformational module, type of activity, intended audience and the European Research Area action it addresses, then examines which of these occur together. The design is a systematic mapping of what alliances produced rather than an evaluation of their impact. The article's findings could not be established here, because the publisher page was inaccessible and only the opening of the abstract is public, so this entry covers the study's question and method only.

deep_analysis.research_question: What have European University alliances contributed to the European Research Area, and how do their outputs map onto ERA actions?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Not established. The publicly available portion of the abstract sets out the evidence gap and the coding approach but stops before results, and no accessible full text or repository copy was found.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Coding of 301 outputs from 32 SwafS-funded European University alliances by transformational module, activity, audience and ERA action, with frequency and co-occurrence analysis. Package contained no source text; partial abstract confirmed online at the publisher.
deep_analysis.qualification: Findings unknown; the study maps outputs rather than measuring impact, so even once available its results would describe activity patterns, not effects on the European Research Area.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Directly addresses whether the European Universities Initiative delivers against European Research Area objectives.

results.reader_title: Corporate research units patent more green technology when the surrounding region already does
results.reader_what: Across 118 European regions, host-region green innovation intensity predicts more green patents by resident corporate research units.
results.reader_why: Policy implication: attracting R&D investment strengthens regional green knowledge bases and cumulative technological capabilities.
results.reader_more: The sample covers 231 leading corporate research spenders with inventive activity spread across 118 European regions between 2000 and 2018. Using fixed-effects logistic and Poisson models, with a control function approach to address reverse causation, the authors find that higher green innovation intensity in a host region is associated with both whether and how many green patents the local research unit files. The association holds only under specific conditions: the host region is foreign to the firm, lies in Europe's core, is environmentally polluting, and regulates more strictly than the firm's home country. Knowledge in the region itself, rather than activity in neighbouring regions, drives the pattern. Patents measure inventive output imperfectly and the data end in 2018.

deep_analysis.research_question: Does green knowledge embedded in a host region shape the green innovation of multinational R&D units located there?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Host-region green innovation intensity is significantly associated with both the occurrence and the count of green patents from resident corporate R&D units, indicating reverse technological spillovers from local context into corporate research, but only where the region is foreign, core, environmentally brown and more strictly regulated than the firm's home country.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Two-step econometric strategy with conditional fixed-effects logistic and Poisson models plus a control function approach and robustness checks, on 231 top R&D firms across 118 European regions, 2000-2018; publisher full text supplied.
deep_analysis.qualification: Results are conditional on specific host-region characteristics, rest on patents as an imperfect proxy for innovation, and remain observational despite endogeneity corrections; data end in 2018.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Bears on whether attracting corporate R&D into European regions builds local green technological capability, a live question for regional and industrial policy.

results.reader_title: Why the EU's digital partnerships with Asian technology powers are underachieving
results.reader_what: Analysis finds partnerships fragmented across institutions and lacking any overarching coordination mechanism or legal architecture.
results.reader_why: Recommends research and innovation collaboration as the least divisive route to long-term interest alignment.
results.reader_more: The report assesses partnerships pursued under the EU's 2025 International Digital Strategy with Japan, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan, covering artificial intelligence, semiconductors, 6G and cybersecurity. Its diagnosis is institutional: many actors with overlapping but misaligned interests, spanning EU bodies, member states, partner ministries, industry and civil society, plus wide variation in depth, from South Korea's full Digital Partnership and Horizon Europe association status to Taiwan's informal channels. Being like-minded, the authors argue, does not guarantee aligned interests, and the stated move from a hub-and-spoke model to a network approach remains aspirational. They recommend widening engagement to smaller firms, start-ups, labour organisations and civil society, and building sectoral groupings among smaller sets of partners.

deep_analysis.research_question: How well are the EU's digital partnerships with like-minded Asian technology powers working, and where do they fall short?
deep_analysis.main_finding: EU-Asia digital partnerships operate in a fragmented ecosystem without unifying institutional or legal architecture, so goals remain underachieved; the authors recommend anchoring alignment in research and innovation collaboration, broadening engagement beyond governments, and using sectoral minilateral formats, with non-recognition-dependent channels for Taiwan.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Policy analysis of EU digital partnership instruments and partner-country arrangements under the 2025 International Digital Strategy; report PDF supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: Assessment and recommendation rather than empirical evaluation; the network model is described as aspirational and the proposed remedies are untested.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Bears directly on EU international research and innovation cooperation as an instrument of digital and technological positioning in Asia.

results.reader_title: Why Europe's weaker economies have not moved into more technologically complex industries
results.reader_what: Sectoral analysis finds peripheral EU economies' industrial mix did not shift toward complex activities, 1995-2020.
results.reader_why: Supports the case that industrial policy must target weaker economies' sectoral composition directly.
results.reader_more: The authors build an index of technological complexity for each economic sector, then use econometric methods to relate sectoral investment to complexity, consumption, interest rates and foreign direct investment across EU countries from 1995 to 2020. Their reading is that divergence inside the Union is structural: an export-led growth model in the north and a credit-supported consumption model in the south left peripheral economies investing in less complex activities, which the authors connect to the break-up of industrial sectors in weaker member states. The complexity index is their own construction, so the results depend on how it is built. The analysis establishes patterns and associations across countries and sectors rather than proving a single cause of divergence.

deep_analysis.research_question: Why have technological and productive disparities widened between EU member states, and what role did sectoral investment play?
deep_analysis.main_finding: The sectoral composition of peripheral EU economies did not shift toward more technologically complex activities over 1995-2020, which the authors link to industrial disintegration in weaker economies and to the need for a redesigned industrial policy.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Author-constructed sectoral technological complexity index combined with econometric analysis of investment, consumption, interest rates and FDI, EU sectors 1995-2020; publisher full text supplied.
deep_analysis.qualification: Findings depend on the construction of the complexity index; the econometrics establish associations across sectors and countries rather than demonstrating causation, and the policy conclusion is the authors' argument.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Provides long-run evidence on intra-EU technological divergence directly relevant to European industrial and cohesion policy design.

results.reader_title: How the European Parliament told the story of AI while writing the AI Act
results.reader_what: Across 500 coded narratives, Parliament's framing of AI stayed stable from 2020 to 2024, even after ChatGPT.
results.reader_why: Documents the framings Parliament used while co-shaping the Act: control, risk-based regulation, joint approach.
results.reader_more: The Narrative Policy Framework breaks a policy story into four parts: characters, plot, setting and moral. The authors applied it to eighteen European Parliament documents from 2020 to 2024, manually coding 500 narratives, and found plots of control and of rising dominating, populated by heroes and beneficiaries rather than villains, presenting AI as both manageable and beneficial. Settings were security, global competition and European legal norms, while the morals centred on risk-based regulation, ethical standards and calls for a joint approach. The striking result is how little changed across four years, including after the release of ChatGPT. The study describes how Parliament talked about AI, which is not the same as showing that this talk determined the legislation.

deep_analysis.research_question: How did Members of the European Parliament construct and evolve policy narratives on AI during the legislative process leading to the AI Act?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Parliamentary AI narratives showed remarkable stability from 2020 to 2024 despite external shocks including the release of ChatGPT, dominated by plots of control and rising with heroes and beneficiaries, settings of security, global competition and European legal norms, and morals of risk-based regulation, ethical standards and a joint European approach.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Narrative Policy Framework applied to a corpus of 18 European Parliament documents from 2020 to 2024 with 500 manually coded narratives. Package contained no source text; the full publisher abstract was recovered online and corroborated by the authors' own summary of the study.
deep_analysis.qualification: Analyses parliamentary discourse rather than legislative causation; the corpus is 18 documents and the coding, while systematic, is manual and interpretive. Interpretation here rests on the abstract rather than the full article.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Illuminates how the EU's co-legislator framed AI during the AI Act process, bearing on the discursive conditions shaping European AI governance.

results.reader_title: What the EU's 2025 export control update means for quantum computing research
results.reader_what: Commentary argues the EU controlled cryogenic components and wafer probers without waiting for multilateral list agreement.
results.reader_why: Licensing requirements could reroute European quantum collaborations, procurement and technology choices.
results.reader_more: Dual-use rules govern goods with both civilian and military applications. The authors' point is procedural as much as technical: the September 2025 update applied uniform EU controls to frontier items such as cryogenic components and wafer probers without waiting for a formal list update from the Wassenaar Arrangement, the consensus forum that has long anchored this area. They read the move as a shift toward plurilateral control aligned with the United States, Japan and Australia. Consequences for research are set out as plausible trajectories, including consortia switching between qubit technologies to avoid licensing hurdles. This is legal commentary written soon after the change, so effects on collaboration and supply chains are anticipated rather than observed.

deep_analysis.research_question: How does the EU's 2025 dual-use regulation update affect quantum technology research, collaboration and supply chains?
deep_analysis.main_finding: By imposing uniform controls on quantum-relevant hardware ahead of multilateral consensus, the EU signalled a shift toward plurilateral export control governance that the authors expect to reshape research collaboration, procurement and technology pathways in quantum computing.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Legal and policy commentary on the September 2025 EU dual-use regulation update set against Wassenaar Arrangement practice and allied controls; publisher open-access text supplied.
deep_analysis.qualification: Written close to the regulatory change; the consequences for collaboration, procurement and technology choice are projections, with illustrative scenarios rather than evidence of adaptation.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Concerns how European export control policy directly conditions access to equipment needed for quantum research and advanced chip fabrication.

results.reader_title: Researchers report that free movement inside the European Research Area breaks down in practice
results.reader_what: A 62-person survey finds administrative obstacles and discriminatory hiring or eligibility rules are the most-cited barriers.
results.reader_why: Written as input to the European Research Area Act expected in late 2026.
results.reader_more: The Fifth Freedom here means free and equal movement of researchers, open access to scientific knowledge, and research funding circulating across the EU. Sixty-two researchers in eleven member states answered three open questions and one closed one, and about 89 per cent backed formal EU recognition of the freedom. Administrative barriers and discriminatory hiring or funding eligibility were each raised by roughly 48 per cent of respondents, with non-recognition of qualifications next at 33 per cent and named as the most-demanded reform. Respondents supplied costed personal cases, including sworn translation fees of two to three hundred euros per diploma and foreign experience counted at half value in salary scales. The authors describe the sample as a self-selected pilot, not statistically representative.

deep_analysis.research_question: What concrete structural barriers do researchers encounter to free movement of researchers, knowledge and funding within the EU?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Rights that exist formally in EU law are described as systematically undermined at operational level by national administrations and universities; administrative burden and discriminatory hiring or eligibility rules dominate, and automatic EU-wide recognition of qualifications is the reform most demanded.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Self-selected survey of 62 researchers across 11 member states, December 2025 to April 2026, with 148 open-text responses thematically coded; report PDF supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: Explicitly a pilot: the sample is small, self-selected and skewed toward Spanish and Danish respondents, so percentages rest on few responses and are not representative of EU researchers.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Produced as direct input to the forthcoming ERA Act and documents specific obstacles to researcher mobility in the European Research Area.

results.reader_title: Turning community visions for 2050 into weighted priorities that city planners can use
results.reader_what: Tested in Chios and Vilnius, the method converts community scenarios into ranked criteria for formal planning.
results.reader_why: Addresses the gap between community climate visioning and formal administrative prioritisation in urban planning.
results.reader_more: The approach has three parts: workshops that build shared scenarios for city futures to 2050; the Analytic Hierarchy Process, a technique that turns pairwise comparisons into numerical weights for criteria chosen by stakeholders; and expert review to check technical feasibility. It was run in two deliberately contrasting Living Labs, the Greek island of Chios and the Lithuanian capital Vilnius. The authors report that the sequence does translate qualitative community narratives into structured, weighted data that fits formal planning cycles. What is demonstrated is that the process runs and produces usable outputs in two settings, not that resulting plans were adopted or that urban climate resilience improved. Two sites also limit how far the approach can be generalised.

deep_analysis.work_kind: peer-reviewed methods study with pilot application
deep_analysis.research_question: How can community-led visioning of climate-resilient urban futures be translated into prioritised inputs that formal city planning can absorb?
deep_analysis.main_finding: A three-stage participatory foresight framework combining co-creative 2050 scenario building, Analytic Hierarchy Process weighting and expert feedback successfully converted qualitative community narratives into structured weighted criteria in two contrasting European city contexts.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Multi-method participatory foresight deployed in two Living Labs (Chios, Greece and Vilnius, Lithuania), combining scenario workshops, AHP prioritisation and expert validation; publisher open-access full text supplied.
deep_analysis.qualification: Demonstrates that the method works and yields planning-ready outputs; it does not show adoption by administrations or any improvement in climate resilience, and rests on two sites.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Offers a transferable participatory foresight and anticipatory governance method tested in two European city contexts.

results.reader_title: Testing whether Europe's food policies add up to a coherent path to transformation
results.reader_what: Analysis finds EU food policy internally incoherent, incremental farm policy reform insufficient, and just-transition governance underdeveloped.
results.reader_why: Assesses Common Agricultural Policy reform against European Environment Agency imaginaries for a sustainable 2050.
results.reader_more: The authors combine participatory foresight with two structured techniques: the X-curve, which sequences the decline of an old system against the rise of a new one, and morphological analysis, which tests whether policy options can be consistently combined. Two expert workshops plus desk research generated transition measures, which were clustered into ten governance dimensions and cross-checked for consistency, yielding four stylised policy mixes. Measured against these, existing EU policy sits closest to a mixed-approaches logic but lacks internal coherence. The judgement that incremental Common Agricultural Policy reform cannot deliver transformation follows from that structured comparison rather than from modelled outcomes. The authors note that fully sequenced roadmaps remain for later work, and the evidence base is two expert workshops.

deep_analysis.research_question: How can foresight and transition research be combined to design internally coherent policy mixes for European food system transformation, and how does current EU policy compare?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Four internally consistent policy mixes were derived; current EU policy most resembles a mixed-approaches logic but lacks internal coherence, incremental Common Agricultural Policy reform is judged insufficient for transformation, and just-transition governance is underdeveloped.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Participatory foresight with two expert workshops and desk research, combined with the X-curve transition model and morphological cross-consistency assessment, anchored on four European Environment Agency imaginaries for 2050; publisher full text supplied.
deep_analysis.qualification: Conclusions rest on expert workshop input and structured consistency assessment, not on modelled or observed policy outcomes; the authors state that fully sequenced roadmaps are left to future research.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Applies foresight methods to assess coherence of an existing major EU policy framework and identifies specific governance gaps.

results.reader_title: A backcasting study of how humanities research evaluation could work by 2040
results.reader_what: Review and backcasting propose three transitions: from indices to impact, toward open science, and toward technology-shaped evaluation.
results.reader_more: Backcasting works backwards from a desired future state to the steps needed to reach it. The authors pair that technique with a scoping review of the literature to sketch humanities research evaluation in 2040, sorting what they find into transitions, requirements and constraints. The three transitions are a move from index-based counting toward impact, from siloed work toward open science, and from tools toward what they term technopoly, meaning evaluation increasingly shaped by technology. They then set out nine policies with twelve first-level and twenty-eight second-level actionable steps. These are recommendations derived from literature and structured reasoning rather than tested interventions, and no particular national system or funder is examined empirically.

deep_analysis.research_question: What approaches, policies, indicators and infrastructures could support a discipline-appropriate framework for evaluating humanities research by 2040?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Three transitions are identified for humanities research evaluation, from index to impact, from siloed practice to open science, and from tools to technology-shaped evaluation, supported by nine proposed policies and forty actionable steps.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Scoping review of the literature integrated with backcasting from a 2040 endpoint; publisher full text supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: Outputs are normative recommendations derived from literature, not empirical findings or tested measures; no specific national or institutional evaluation system is assessed.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Relevant to ongoing research assessment reform debates, though the study is not Europe-specific and makes no claim about European systems.

results.reader_title: Experts map what would have to change for a post-growth Europe to be feasible
results.reader_what: Participants judge most current trends to block strong sustainability while identifying specific openings for intervention.
results.reader_why: Produces scenarios and futures statements for Europe under post-growth rather than growth assumptions.
results.reader_more: Post-growth covers economic models such as degrowth, doughnut economics and wellbeing economics that aim for development within planetary limits rather than expanding output. The method the authors call integral foresight combines a review of literature on possible futures with horizon scanning and scenario building, run as multiple online rounds among researchers, subject experts and futurists. The output is a filtered, refined and categorised set of futures statements spanning social, technological, economic, environmental, political, legal, ethical and demographic dimensions, plus scenarios built on differing assumptions. The conclusions are expert expectations elicited through a structured process, not forecasts or evidence about what will occur. Participants were recruited for their engagement with post-growth and sustainability, which shapes the range of views represented.

deep_analysis.research_question: What trends, weak signals and pathways bear on the feasibility of post-growth futures for Europe?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Experts expect many current trends to obstruct strong sustainability in Europe, while judging that intervention points exist and that desirable post-growth alternatives remain reachable, notably through democratic stewardship of nature.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Integral foresight process combining post-growth and sustainable development literature with horizon scanning and scenario building across multiple online interactive rounds with researchers, experts and futurists; publisher full text supplied.
deep_analysis.qualification: Findings are structured expert expectations rather than forecasts or empirical results, and participants were selected for existing engagement with post-growth and sustainability topics.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Develops explicitly European future alternatives under post-growth assumptions, offering scenario material for European sustainability and economic policy debate.

results.reader_title: The same foresight methods do different institutional work in different governance systems
results.reader_what: Comparative study concludes EU foresight functions as networked, anticipatory infrastructure rather than isolated forecasting techniques.
results.reader_why: Covers ESPAS, the Strategic Foresight Reports, the Better Regulation Toolbox and Open Strategic Autonomy.
results.reader_more: The argument is that a method is never institutionally neutral: the same scenario or expert exercise does different work depending on the governance setting it sits in. The authors distinguish technocratic, market-managerial, networked and anticipatory logics, and map functions onto each, from expert prioritisation in the first to strategic positioning in the second, stakeholder alignment and legitimacy in the third, and early warning and policy adaptation in the fourth. The EU is the focal case, with Japan and South Korea used as deliberate contrasts rather than as a symmetrical comparison. Evidence comes from bibliometric mapping of Scopus, semantic analysis of method terms and manual validation of 68 publications, so the study characterises how foresight is positioned rather than measuring its influence on decisions.

deep_analysis.work_kind: peer-reviewed comparative conceptual and bibliometric study
deep_analysis.research_question: How do foresight methods perform different institutional functions across different governance logics, and where does EU strategic foresight sit?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Foresight methods are not institutionally neutral: their function shifts across technocratic, market-managerial, networked and anticipatory settings, and the EU shows the most developed combination of networked and anticipatory functions, making its foresight a governance infrastructure rather than a set of forecasting techniques.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Contrastive case design with the EU as focal case and Japan and South Korea as contrasts, combining exploratory Scopus bibliometrics, VOSviewer semantic analysis, manual validation of 68 publications and qualitative interpretation; publisher full text supplied.
deep_analysis.qualification: Deliberately asymmetric comparison based on literature and documents; it characterises institutional framing and does not measure whether foresight changed decisions or outcomes.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Maps the EU's own strategic foresight machinery, including ESPAS, Strategic Foresight Reports and the Better Regulation Toolbox, as an integrated governance capability.

results.reader_title: A proposed software architecture to make scenario planning practical for smaller companies
results.reader_what: Design paper proposes a modular AI-assisted scenario pipeline with guided wizard and shared knowledge backbone.
results.reader_more: Scenario management means building and maintaining alternative pictures of the future in order to test strategy against them. The authors start from the observation that smaller firms rarely have the time, expertise or tooling to do this well, and that available tools are fragmented. Their proposal pairs a guided wizard for non-specialists with a fuller environment for experienced users, both drawing on a shared knowledge store so that one exercise can feed later ones instead of ending as a standalone project. Recording where each input came from and keeping a person in the loop are intended to preserve explainability and human judgement. This is an architectural proposal presented at a design conference; it has not been implemented with firms or evaluated against outcomes.

deep_analysis.research_question: How can scenario management be made feasible for small and medium-sized enterprises that lack time, expertise and integrated tools?
deep_analysis.main_finding: The authors propose a modular, provenance-aware and AI-enabled foresight pipeline combining a guided wizard and an expert environment on a shared knowledge backbone, intended to turn one-off scenario projects into reusable organisational knowledge while keeping humans in the loop.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Conceptual architecture and design pattern description; publisher abstract and paper text supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: A proposal only: no implementation, user trial or evaluation with enterprises is reported, so claimed reductions in effort and improvements in reuse are design intentions.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Concerns foresight capability in smaller firms and the use of AI in scenario methods, though the paper makes no specifically European claim.

results.reader_title: Building a regulatory culture that anticipates innovation instead of chasing it
results.reader_what: Article argues foresight, policy labs, pilot regulation and sandboxes should be integrated into one regulatory toolbox.
results.reader_why: Examines regulatory sandboxes as an EU policy tool, including their use in the AI Act.
results.reader_more: Regulatory lag is the gap between technology moving and law catching up. The author's case is that the remedy is not a single well-crafted statute but a standing capability: strategic foresight, iterative policy development, and learning from controlled trials. She surveys instruments already in use, including policy labs that develop rules with those affected, pilot regulation, experimentation and regulatory sandboxes in which firms test products under supervision, and argues they remain scattered rather than assembled into a coherent toolbox. The sandbox provisions of the EU AI Act are examined as the leading example. This is a legal and policy argument, so the claim that integration would improve regulation is reasoned rather than shown through evaluation.

deep_analysis.research_question: What does building an agile but robust anticipatory governance culture for regulating technological innovation involve?
deep_analysis.main_finding: A range of anticipatory instruments, including regulatory foresight, iterative policy development, policy labs, pilot regulation and sandboxes, are already used inventively but in isolation; the author argues they should be integrated systemically into jurisdictions' regulatory toolboxes rather than pursued as one-off fixes.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Doctrinal and policy analysis surveying anticipatory regulatory instruments, with attention to EU sandbox practice including the AI Act; publisher open-access full text supplied.
deep_analysis.qualification: Normative legal argument rather than empirical evaluation; no evidence is presented that integrating these tools improves regulatory outcomes.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Addresses how the EU regulates emerging technology and situates AI Act sandboxes within a wider anticipatory governance approach.

results.reader_title: Borrowing from deliberative democracy and philosophy of science to give foresight epistemic standing
results.reader_what: Article argues reason-giving deliberation and perspectival realism can ground foresight's authority alongside established scientific disciplines.
results.reader_why: Addresses why foresight struggles for epistemic authority when set against established disciplines in policymaking.
results.reader_more: Perspectival realism is a position in philosophy of science holding that knowledge advances through interaction between distinct epistemic communities, each working with its own models. The author borrows it to argue that foresight produces what he calls modal models, structured accounts of what is possible, which can legitimately sit alongside other forms of evidence in policy. From deliberative democracy he takes the emphasis on pluralism and on giving reasons, presenting this as what lends foresight depth in public debate rather than merely generating options. The paper is a theoretical contribution: it offers a justification for foresight's standing in the policy process rather than evidence that adopting this framing changes practice.

deep_analysis.research_question: How can foresight establish epistemic authority in public policy alongside the natural and social sciences?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Deliberative democracy supplies an account of how reason-giving adds epistemic depth to foresight, while perspectival realism recasts foresight's outputs as modal models produced by an epistemic community, together offering a basis for foresight's standing in evidence-based policymaking.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Conceptual argument drawing on political theory and philosophy of science; publisher open-access full text supplied in package.
deep_analysis.qualification: Theoretical and normative; no empirical test of whether this framing improves foresight's uptake or influence in policy processes.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Concerns the credibility of foresight as an input to public policy, a standing question for institutionalised foresight, though not EU-specific.

results.reader_title: Using functional analysis and text mining to identify emerging technologies
results.reader_what: Paper proposes analysing what a technology does, rather than what it is called, to detect emerging technologies.
results.reader_why: Authors argue the approach makes technology foresight affordable for small and medium-sized firms.
results.reader_more: Functional analysis asks what function an artefact performs for a user, instead of describing it by its components or its label. The authors apply that lens to technology foresight, combining it with natural language processing tuned for patent documents and with expert domain knowledge. They use it to look for development patterns, spot missing elements and potential failure points, and to strengthen conventional bibliometric approaches such as S-curve analysis. Their affordability argument rests on patent and publication data being cheap and widely available, so the constraint is analytical capacity rather than access. This is a 2016 methodological proposal demonstrated by its own authors, and the text-mining techniques available have changed substantially since.

deep_analysis.research_question: Can functional analysis, combined with text mining of patents, provide a cheaper and more user-centred way to identify emerging technologies?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Applying functional analysis to technology foresight, integrated with a patent-tailored natural language processing toolchain and expert knowledge, is proposed as a way to detect development patterns and emerging technologies while lowering cost enough for smaller firms to use.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Methodological development combining functional analysis, bibliometric S-curve analysis and NLP applied to patent documents, with illustrative application; publisher open-access full text supplied.
deep_analysis.qualification: Proposal demonstrated by its own authors without independent validation or benchmarking against alternative methods; published in 2016, so the text-mining component predates current techniques.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Offers a technology foresight method for identifying emerging technologies, with an explicit claim about accessibility for smaller firms.
